beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a title.

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent isn't as simple as sharing a licence, and there are four ways to do it. I don't yet know what any of them cost.

beats.trigger: a tool people can open and mostly don't
beats.got: I'm asked for an example of paid-for tools nobody uses. I have several. The collaboration suite is one.

beats.trigger: **Interview** for the job a teammate is trying to get done before deciding what to share
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a list of verbs with no cost, risk or payback attached.

beats.trigger: Your challenge memory has been working for you for days.
beats.got: This assumes I have an agent with a memory that has been running for days. I don't. I'd have to borrow someone else's setup.

beats.trigger: The question arrives on its own: *could this help someone else?*
beats.got: Nothing new. A long intro with a Christensen reference and no figure.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The agent reads my files and writes up one person's job, and I check it's specific. That is a test I can apply, and it's my own material.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Picking a tool because it fits the infrastructure is the mistake I've watched three programmes make. The module names it. Still no cost per option, though.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: Nothing new. A handover to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: **Time:** 23 minutes.
beats.got: There's a stated time box. Good. I know what I'm in for.

beats.trigger: The obstacle is usually not the first technical limitation a builder sees.
beats.got: The real blocker is more often governance or trust than technology. In my case it's IT not approving the tool for finance data.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: It flags unowned roles as the risk, before I have to raise it. That is the board question: who owns it and who answers for it.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact
beats.got: Nothing new. Another handover.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until tested. I can agree with that.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Name the conditions under which people would drop their current method. That's a decent business question, but nothing here is quantified.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem followed by one named person and one test. That's concrete, and cheap to run.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Interview for the outcome first, pick against it, and test the switch rather than the solution. Choosing a tool because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.

beats.trigger: Sharing an agent runs into one law.
beats.got: A lecture is starting and I'm told there is one law.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: You can copy the context, the boundary and the checks, but not the person who answers for the result. That is exactly what audit asks me about.

beats.trigger: Different challenges want different strategies, and different people absorb different ones.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's the four strategies again, in a paragraph.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Seats bought and people actually using it get reported as one adoption number. That is my licence misconception, and it's exactly how I'd have read a vendor dashboard.

beats.trigger: Then name what would have had to change in people's weeks for them to use it.
beats.got: I should list what would have to change in people's weeks, not what was switched on. Mostly that's people plan, not IT.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A real story where a good proposal got no decision because urgency moved on. I've sat in that meeting. It isn't about my topic, but it is credible, and it's candid.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The incumbent is a spreadsheet or a colleague that works well enough, and the new thing has to beat it. That's how I'd frame any investment.

beats.trigger: Send that person one message asking for twenty minutes on how they do the job now.
beats.got: Monday is one message and twenty minutes. That's cheap enough that I'd do it.

take_homes: Seats switched on and people actually using the tool are two different numbers. I'll ask for usage, not licence counts, in any AI business case.
You can copy an agent's context, boundary and checks but not who answers for it. If no one owns it, it isn't ready to share.
Before approving any rollout, ask who the person is, how they do the job today, and what would make them drop it.

monday.move: Ask my controller for twenty minutes on how month-end variance commentary gets done today, before I show her any agent. Also ask IT what the approval path is for finance data.
monday.who: My controller; IT lead as a second message
monday.stop_condition: If the variance commentary takes her under an hour and she's happy with it, I drop it. If IT has no approval path, I escalate rather than keep trying.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data.

misconception.why: I walked in thinking AI is a licence you buy. The point that access is a switch and absorption is a separate thing in other people's weeks undercut that, and the unowned roles in the people plan showed that someone has to carry it. I still don't see a cost figure, so I'm not fully convinced.

one_line: Better than a demo day, because it names why bought tools go unused. But it never put a price or a payback on anything, and I'd still have to build the number myself.
